title: Stanford Robotics Seminar ENGR319 | Spring 2026 | Unlocking Autonomous Medical Robotics
transcriptText:
Thanks, everybody,
for being here.
I'm really glad to
be back at Stanford,
where I did my PhD,
and really talking
about a body of work that has
been spanning at least 10 years
but has really taken
off in a new direction,
that I'm really excited to
cover throughout the course
of the talk today.
And it's really going
to be going over
this idea of trying to unlock
the concept of autonomous
surgical robots.
I want to start with this idea
of, what are robots actually
leveraged for?
And I think one perspective
that you can take
is that it is really
to meet this growing
need for skilled labor.
And this need is happening
across all kinds of industries,
of which health care is one that
is both significantly impacted
but also an industry that we
absolutely are intrinsically
tied to every one of us.
If we look at the shortage
of health care workers,
in this country alone,
we're looking at, currently,
numbers of tens of
thousands of surgeons
that are not sufficiently
trained in terms
of meeting the needs of
the patient population.
Simultaneously, we're
seeing shortages
of hundreds of
thousands of nurses
necessary to meet the demands
of the health care population.
And so with this
observation, robots
are actually a very,
very strong opportunity
to come in and provide
significant value.
They have some very
nice properties,
such as they don't get tired.
I mean, they need
charging, of course,
but they don't get tired.
They're available 24/7.
They have a precision that often
can go beyond human capability.
We talk about CAD
and CAM precisions
from the machinist point of
view in submillimeter ranges.
And we could, in
certain platforms,
get that type of precision
as well in robotics.
The very interesting thing
about robotics as well as
a platform technology
for scaling skilled labor
is that, in the health
care practice today,
we have this notion of one
physician or one nurse training
side by side with another
physician or nurse.
And this is a very
linear increase
in making that skilled
labor group grow.
However, for
robotics, these can be
conducted on a
fleet-wide update basis,
just like autonomous vehicles.
I'm not sure how many people
drive Teslas in this room.
But of course, you can
have an example today
where, overnight, you will
get a new software update,
and the system will
have acquired some sort
of new autonomous skill.
Finally, this idea of
programmable expertise
is really interesting.
And how many people have gone
into health care settings
and wondering, well, what
is the quality of care I'm
getting in this setting
versus another setting
or another individual?
In this case, you can program
uniformity of expertise
across these platforms.
I want to give an idea of
where current paradigms
of medical robotics are today.
This is a da Vinci
surgical system.
It is a teleoperated
surgical robot
that has tools that
go inside your body.
And the surgeon
operates these tools
using a joystick
console, as shown here.
And the tools inside your
body move, basically,
directly proportional to
the movement of the surgeon.
This robot has been around for
well over 25, if not 30 years,
at this point.
And if we look at where
the landscape of surgical
robotics today, it's
really exploded.
And this is just a snapshot
of all the surgical robotics
out there.
There are a significantly
higher number of robots
that I couldn't put on the page.
But the point I want to make
is that all of these robots
are teleoperated today.
They have zero inherent skill.
The skill is coming
from the surgeon.
And it does make surgeons
more precise and less tired.
But what it doesn't do is
it doesn't help us address
the population crisis issue.
It does not help
us do more surgery.
And in fact, when you're
doing robotic surgery,
oftentimes the
surgical team that's
required to perform
the procedure
requires more
personnel than if you
were to do it without a robot.
Now, if you look
on the other side,
where there is autonomous
robots being deployed,
it's manufacturing.
And in manufacturing, it's all
rigid, preprogrammed motions.
They operate in a very
structured environment.
They require extensive
setup and human oversight.
But they do excel at speed,
precision, and repeatability.
This is autonomy but
in an unskilled way.
So what if we try to merge
the concepts of autonomy
and surgical robotics?
This concept is
actually not new at all.
If you can believe
it, this is concepts
that have been dating back
many decades, both from things
like ROBODOC that was used
for orthopedic surgery
and doing small
alignments for implants,
to AESOP, which is a
voice-controlled robot that
holds a surgical camera
for laparoscopic surgery,
to methods from university labs
that have looked at using, what
is very popular today,
concepts of imitation
learning, or learning from
demonstration, to show things
like autonomous suturing.
So all of this has been a
progression of new techniques
back in the day that
have been applied
over and over to try to address
this issue of surgical autonomy.
And in certain cases, we've been
able to show some successes.
But if we look at where
are we recently today
in terms of general
robot autonomy,
we're looking at these
ideas of large foundation
models or
vision-language-action models,
which usually require
large data sets,
which is massive data
collection at scale,
or developing what's called
world models, like simulations
or generative models
of the world, that
are trying to describe how
the world evolves over time.
And what we see in
this space right now
is a large variability
between accuracy and success.
And so there's a
lot of tasks that
are shown that can
be very successful
at decent accuracies in the mid
to high 90 percentage range.
But there's also many that
are failing dramatically.
And all of these
foundation models
have been developed in what I
would say is relatively clean
and controlled settings,
where stakes are low.
The environment
can be easily reset
and for the tasks in which the
demonstrators are abundant.
So people that can sit
down at a console and just
show a robot how to
fold a piece of laundry.
Almost anybody can do that.
But surgical robotics
has that issue
of none of those properties
really exist for surgery
so that you have scarce data.
The setting cannot
be controlled.
The setting cannot
be easily reset.
When you're doing a surgery, you
can't roll back time normally.
Safety is absolutely critical.
So few demonstrators--
we already talked
about the lack of surgeons.
So there's even
fewer demonstrators,
and there's very low incentives
for them to be sitting and doing
demonstrations for
a robot learner.
Data collection in
these situations
is basically at the
lowest priority.
You're usually trying
to address a patient
and not to address the
machine learning algorithm.
And finally, world
models right now
have no concrete
path to maturity.
Given that there
is a limited data,
that data is protected
behind and reasonably so
behind privacy laws.
And so how else can
we approach autonomy?
And so we can look back
at what I would say
is the foundational pillars
of autonomous robots.
And I would say
that there's four
that I would categorize as--
one is perception, seeing
and perceiving the world
and feeling the world.
Second one is modeling
and simulation,
so understanding rough
models of how things move,
the general physics of the
world at a small scale.
Planning, understanding
how to make decisions,
given that you how the world
evolves, and then control,
executing those actions
in a precise way.
And altogether, in
various types of methods,
we can bring these
all together to get
what we call embodied
intelligence and autonomy.
So at my lab at UC
San Diego, we have
been playing around with
these four pillars quite a lot
and trying to build
up the technology
to make surgical
autonomy possible.
And we've looked
at a large range
of different areas of autonomous
suturing to assistance,
to deformable modeling and
probing to very specific robot
applications, like
biopsy and cancer.
And I think what
we've learned and what
I feel like I've learned over
the time is that at least one
very viable path to unlocking
autonomous, intelligent robots
in surgery is a structured path
of building context awareness,
moving towards incorporating
multiple knowledge cues to build
on this knowledge, to
be a lifelong learner
and then finding
common embodiments
so that we can deploy
it at a larger scale.
So I want to cover these
ideas during this talk.
So for achieving context
awareness, what I'm really
talking about is perception.
So robot autonomy,
in my opinion,
can only be as good as its
perception and its ability
to recognize and
understand the world.
And only recently have we
been able to get techniques
very much on the backbone
of large data collection
and foundational
models to segment
the world, identify,
localize, and track targets.
These are just two examples
of the state of the art.
And I'm sure that these will
change within the next six
months to something
even more powerful
as the field progresses
in computer vision.
One thing I will say, though,
is that surgical robotics
is one of the
hardest environments
to work in for these
perception tasks,
because oftentimes
when you're trying
to understand the
surgical environment,
you have typically a very
narrow field of view.
You don't have context
understanding globally.
You have bad or no
depth measurements.
Usually, you have either a
single camera to understand
in 2D what the space is like.
But you have to infer depth
from things like shadows
and even understanding
of the anatomy that
is being shown to you.
So this is a lot
of prior knowledge
you need to have
built up over time.
Or in the other case, you have
cameras that are stereo cameras.
So you have two cameras that
can do perception, stereo
perception.
But the baseline between
the two eyes of the camera
are so tight that you have
very poor depth perception.
You also, like I said,
have specular reflections
from fluids, blood.
And there's smoke when you're
cutting through tissue.
You're always kind of
cutting through the scene
with large instruments.
And so it's always
occluding your view.
Everything is deformable.
Sometimes it's hard to find
an anchor point in the scene
to know where things are static.
And like I said, there's
insufficient data
to train modern neural models.
And all of this is
wrapped around the fact
that whatever we
learn, oftentimes we
want millimeter precision.
So how can we break this down?
Because this is a very
challenging problem.
And I will say we spent all
of the last 10 to 11 years
I've been at UCSD just
continuously working
on this problem.
And it can be broken down
into several categories.
Here is the four main ones,
which is precise robot
proprioception.
That is the idea
that, as a robot,
it has to know exactly
where its hands are
or its instruments are in space.
Precise object
localization-- it has
to know exactly where
objects are in space
relative to those instruments.
3D scene reconstruction--
understanding the background
of what it's interacting with.
And especially in
surgery, the it
is a continuous gradient from
foreground to background.
And so understanding 3D scene
reconstruction and then scene
fusion so that despite the fact
that you have a very narrow
point of view, over time,
as the camera moves around,
you get a better sense of
where you are in space.
So we have done a lot of work in
this area across surgical tool
tracking, things
like needle tracking,
even suture thread tracking for
the explicit purpose of being
able to very precisely get
our robot instruments to grab
objects in space.
And we have also done the third
and fourth tasks of 3D scene
reconstruction and fusion, which
is really about reconstructing
an entirely deformable
environment.
I wanted to spend a
little bit of time
on this, because reconstructing
a deformable scene
is really important, not only
from the perspective of being
able to track where anatomy
is as you manipulate it
and move it around.
And that's obviously important
when you're doing something
like excising a tumor.
And you want to be able to
make sure you enough margin
around the tumor as you
cut and release it so
that you don't miss any lesion.
But it's also important
from the perspective
of physics understanding.
And so if we start
with this technology
that we had developed
over many years
to get deformable reconstruction
from cameras of the scene,
how can we move that into
a useful set of information
to inform how do we do
cutting and dissection?
So if we go from vision and
understanding of the scene
to then instruct a
robot how to cut,
we need something
in the between.
And that is our
model of physics.
So what is absolutely
necessary in this scenario
is this understanding of
the physics and mechanics
of deforming tissue.
So this idea is generally
coined as digital twinning.
And there's many techniques
to do digital twinning.
One technique that we were very
excited about when we started
was this method that was
developed in computer graphics
called position-based dynamics.
And the idea of
position-based dynamics
was that you would simulate
a deformable scene using
particles.
And you would run the
particle interactions
using a set of constraints that
define how those particles would
either bounce off each other
or constrain to each other.
And the most important aspect
of this was, number one,
it could run faster
than real time.
And number two, it could satisfy
position constraints exactly.
So the first one I'll explain,
if you have a simulator that
can run faster than
real time, then
that means that you can
simulate many possibilities
and evaluate all possibilities
of interaction with a tissue
without actually
interacting with it
and waiting for a long
time to figure out
what the consequences are.
So at the end of the day,
you can close a loop on that
and create a
model-based controller
that is very standard in
classical robot control theory.
So that is a very, very
useful-- and actually,
it's like a property that
is absolutely necessary
to apply those techniques.
The second property of
position-based dynamics
was that we could
take what we observed
from the cameras,
which generated
this topological surface map.
And we could force, in one shot,
the simulator to match that.
And that means that we don't
have to do many, many iterations
to get the matching to occur.
And therefore, it keeps that
faster than real-time simulation
from slowing down.
So one of the things that
we immediately found out
was that if you go into a
surgical type of environment
and you recreate the
environment from scratch,
and then you immediately
try to simulate it,
because you're recreating the
digital twin from just a surface
image, you have to guess what
is happening under the surface.
And so right when
the model tries
to move the tissue
in simulation,
the simulation won't
match real life.
And so what we can do is, to
correct for this behavior,
we can use something called
differentiable rendering.
And in a differentiable
rendering,
the idea is that we can
take observations that
are streaming in from a camera.
And we can look at how
those observations match up
to the simulation.
We can get a loss between the
observations of the simulation
and the camera image.
And then we can back
propagate that loss
to find how the simulation
simulator should change
to make it match the real life.
And in this case, what needs
to be changed in the simulator
is the mechanics
properties of those tissues
as well as things like
if the camera moved.
Now, what we can
see if we do that is
that we can get the simulator
to continuously match
the observations coming
from streaming video.
And you can actually get
a significant decrease
in the amount of prediction
error from your model
before you do this iterative
correction to after.
And the difference is
from several millimeters,
5 millimeters down to sub 2
millimeter error accuracy.
So this is for
surfaces that are kind
of mesh-like and
topological in that nature.
But we can also do it for
things like rope-like objects.
So this is taking
an image of a rope
and having a initialization
of a simulator of that rope,
pulling on the rope and
understanding and learning
the physics properties
of that rope, especially
its viscoelasticity.
You can imagine that this is
applied in surgery to things
like manipulating
vessels and understanding
the stiffness of those vessels,
which is, of course, important
for safety.
We can do it for fluids as well.
Fluids is just the extreme
end of a soft body.
And this is just
an example of us
looking at a video of
chocolate milk being poured.
And we're trying to estimate
the viscosity of that chocolate
milk.
Now, of course, how does
that relate to surgery?
Well, we were very interested
in hemorrhage control.
And so when you see a
hemorrhaging happening,
there's going to
be a flow of blood.
And it's going to start pooling.
And what we were
very interested in
was to use a very quick
understanding of the properties
of that fluid to use closed-loop
control to suction up
the fluid as fast as possible.
And so if we define
a problem like that,
it becomes an optimal
control problem.
And so we basically did
model predictive control
on this, where the model itself
was this physics simulation.
And then another kind of a thing
that was very important to us
was to uncover where
connections are occurring.
One of the hallmarks
of surgery is
that you're going to be
dissecting through tissue.
And you have to have to find
where the tissue is connected.
And one of the ways that we
found that tissues could--
one of the ways we found that
tissues could show that they
were connected was
when we pulled on it,
we could see that the texture
from the side we're pulling on
at some point would have a
sharp discontinuity in terms
of translation.
And so when we see that
sharp discontinuity,
that shows us that there is a
connection in those locations.
That's shown on the
left-hand side in the purple.
What we can do as well is to
wrap this up in a Bayesian
inferencing framework,
where not only do
we have a guess of where
the connections are,
but we can attribute
uncertainty as to where
we think those connections are.
And once you have a
measure of uncertainty,
you can incorporate that into a
safety-aware control approach.
And this is an example,
at least in simulation,
of how a robot
autonomously would
wrap a safety-aware
controller around tugging
on tissue to find
out where things
are connected before cutting.
So in this case, the
simulation of moving
around this connected tissue
is where the robot effector
doesn't know that it's kind of
connected on the red regions.
And as it's moving around,
it reveals those red regions
are connected.
And it will try to maximize the
amount of information gained
about other regions
while making sure it's
below some energy threshold,
which is basically
the tearing energy.
And so given all
of this, you can
imagine that you've found a
place where it's connected.
Now it's time to cut.
And so here's the example of us
doing this type of procedure.
I should have mentioned
that all of these videos
are butcher shop meats.
Yeah, probably should
mentioned that ahead of time.
But this is all on the
bench type of work.
So this is an example
of our robot learning
how to basically
peel back tissue
to expose the region of cutting
for a secondary cutting arm
to come in.
And this is all autonomous based
on model predictive control
methods.
Now, one of the
things that is what
is called an emergent property
in modern foundation models
from robotics is this
idea of recovery.
And so if you query a
foundation model today
and it fails at a certain
task, oftentimes people
will show you that the policy
will go back in and try again,
which is really great
as an emergent property.
But it's also completely
uncontrolled in the sense
that there is no, actually,
guarantee that the robot will
come in and try again.
It's relatively random
chance at least currently.
But if you have an explicit
model about where things--
if you have an explicit
model about what's
happening in the environment
and you've tied it to physics,
you can query in that model
whether it's failed or not.
And then you can go in, and you
can be targeted and basically
have surgical precision,
for lack of a better word,
of where to attack next and
perform the procedure so
that you complete the task.
One of these cases
is where you're
trying to cut through
a piece of tissue,
and you have failed the cut.
And if you look at using a model
like this real-to-sim digital
twinning framework and applying
this continuous iterative
matching routine
to it, you can see
that we can model where
our cuts were effective
and where they were not.
And we can then go
in and specifically
cut those regions out, all
in an automatic fashion.
And so here's this is an
example of one of our autonomous
routines cutting
through this chicken.
Yeah.
Now, all of these are
techniques that we've built up
from the vision and the modeling
and the planning and control
side, basically, this toolbox
that we can put together
for developing
autonomous surgery.
And by advancing these tools,
we can improve the capabilities
of these tools individually.
And we can strengthen their
reliability over time.
And by assembling these tools
in different configurations,
we can broaden the
capabilities of what
we can automate while explicitly
retaining explainability, which
is extremely important in
automating robotic surgery,
where you have to be able to
say, what is my robot doing?
Is it going to be safe?
And making sure that you, as
the supervisory individual,
is in control at all times,
and it's not really the robot.
So that's great.
But everything I've showed you
really has been, piece by piece,
engineered together.
And so every single task,
you have to hand engineer.
And so would there be a better
way to scale this over time?
And so given a set of
behaviors or policies,
we want to find a good way to
sequence them and combine them
in a way that can be
learned autonomously
and also in a way
that can be learned--
in which new skills
can be added over time.
And so this idea is
called lifelong learning.
And it's still a very
early field of research.
And there is still a great
deal to explore here.
One approach that my
lab has been looking at
is this idea of combining all
of these learned or engineered
behaviors into a neural network
that glues them together.
And so we call this
knowledge-grounded reinforcement
learning.
And in this case, we have
basically knowledge modules,
as you can see in the green.
And those knowledge modules
contain the actual behavior
of a small set of behaviors.
And those behaviors
could be very different.
So some behaviors
could be a robot camera
that's moving around
to scan something.
Or it could be a robot tool
coming in and doing a cut,
picking up objects,
transferring objects from hands,
many different
kinds of behaviors
that you can incorporate.
And then the idea
here is that using
a very sparse neural network
architecture, where there
is a little bit of
weighting that's
used to glue these
knowledge modules together,
you can create a framework
where, through reinforcement
learning, it learns by
itself how these knowledge
modules should be combined
so that you can get a longer
sequence of tasks done.
So for example, you have a
knowledge set that you learned.
In this case, we
learned it using
reinforcement learning in a
simple simulated environment.
We specifically
looked at a task that
was part of what's
called the fundamentals
of laparoscopic surgery,
which is like an exam,
basically, that laparoscopic
surgeons have to take to prove
that they are able to do
the laparoscopic surgery
effectively.
And so these are things like
picking up and grasping,
suturing needles, moving
blocks from peg to peg,
transferring objects between
hands and so on and so forth.
So using reinforcement learning,
we can deploy them in real life
and show that they
are effective,
going from the simulator
to the real world.
And then using the
same kind of approach,
we can show that it can learn
to sequence the set of steps
for doing Multithrow suturing.
So with this kind of
ability, it enables,
I think, a very interesting
framework for building autonomy.
But one thing that I've
recognized we've struggled with
is that everything
we've shown has
been on this da Vinci platform.
And there's all these
kinds of robots out there.
And does this mean that we
have to do the same thing
for every single robot?
Is there a best way to scale
the usefulness of robot autonomy
for health care when the
robots are so diverse?
And so of course, recently,
as everybody knows,
there has been a very
significant interest
in humanoid platforms.
And so back in about
a year and a half ago,
all of these humanoid
platforms were coming out.
And they were doing
backflips and Kung
Fu, a lot of things
that didn't really
speak to me about how
is this forwarding
our society in a meaningful way.
And of course, there was
interest in their use
in home care,
although a lot of it
was also in their
use in manufacturing,
but not a single video
or instance of anybody
talking about its use in
the health care system.
So what we did was
that we went out,
and we deployed one of
these humanoid robots
through mostly
teleoperation-- and I'll
get to exactly how much
teleoperation later--
but through mostly teleoperation
in as many hospital
settings as we could.
And so this is what
that project led to.
This robot, we named Surgie.
Surgie is a humanoid robot with
a humanoid five-fingered hands.
We specifically looked at common
procedures that you would see,
and especially in
emergency scenarios
where we could justify that
having a robot present to do
a procedure when there
wasn't a physician present
had significant value
and had a lot of--
it was easy to justify.
Some examples of tasks
that are actually
challenging for nonskilled
individuals to perform,
this is an example
of intubation.
You have, obviously,
only a few minutes
to get intubated before
you suffocate and die.
And so if you're in
a situation where
you can either trust your robot
to try to do it autonomously
or in teleoperated or
just not have that,
then I'm sure you would
take the robot option.
So here are just
examples of what
we were able to do through
this surgery platform.
And I think what this
is really getting
towards is that
there is a real value
proposition for humanoid robots
in a health care setting.
Because if we think about
the surgical robot I showed,
the Intuitive system, right now,
each system is over $3 million.
And there's very few hospitals,
even in the United States,
that can afford more than
one or two da Vinci systems.
And to think about the
remote communities that
have limited access and
capital and resources,
and that is only for
laparoscopic surgery.
You can also think
about scenarios
where you have surgical teams,
where a surgeon is working side
by side with another surgeon.
And this is actually more common
than just having one surgeon
operating in an operating room.
You're usually working in pairs.
If you're in an environment
where you do not
have enough surgeons,
then you are actually
taking somebody that's skilled
that could be treating somebody
else and putting them in
a scenario where they're
doing very relatively limited
skill-assistive tasks,
like holding a camera or
retracting tissue and holding it
back so that the primary
surgeon can get a good view.
And you can think about
circulating nurses.
You can think about scrub
nurses handing off instruments.
You can think about
ultrasound techs.
All of these
applications, there's
really not that
much justification
for having another
robot and another robot
and another robot that a
hospital would have to purchase
and get approvals for to run
through the entire pipeline
so that they have
sufficient coverage of all
these application areas.
But of course, humanoid robots
with enough skill can do this.
So we look at ideas of remote
surgeon avatars, autonomous

segments.text: Thanks, everybody, for being here. I'm really glad to be back at Stanford, where I did my PhD, and really talking about a body of work that has been spanning at least 10 years but has really taken off in a new direction, that I'm really excited to

cover throughout the course of the talk today. And it's really going to be going over this idea of trying to unlock the concept of autonomous surgical robots. I want to start with this idea of, what are robots actually leveraged for?

And I think one perspective that you can take is that it is really to meet this growing need for skilled labor. And this need is happening across all kinds of industries, of which health care is one that is both significantly impacted

but also an industry that we absolutely are intrinsically tied to every one of us. If we look at the shortage of health care workers, in this country alone, we're looking at, currently, numbers of tens of thousands of surgeons that are not sufficiently

trained in terms of meeting the needs of the patient population. Simultaneously, we're seeing shortages of hundreds of thousands of nurses necessary to meet the demands of the health care population. And so with this observation, robots are actually a very,

very strong opportunity to come in and provide significant value. They have some very nice properties, such as they don't get tired. I mean, they need charging, of course, but they don't get tired. They're available 24/7. They have a precision that often

can go beyond human capability. We talk about CAD and CAM precisions from the machinist point of view in submillimeter ranges. And we could, in certain platforms, get that type of precision as well in robotics. The very interesting thing

about robotics as well as a platform technology for scaling skilled labor is that, in the health care practice today, we have this notion of one physician or one nurse training side by side with another physician or nurse. And this is a very linear increase

in making that skilled labor group grow. However, for robotics, these can be conducted on a fleet-wide update basis, just like autonomous vehicles. I'm not sure how many people drive Teslas in this room. But of course, you can have an example today

where, overnight, you will get a new software update, and the system will have acquired some sort of new autonomous skill. Finally, this idea of programmable expertise is really interesting. And how many people have gone into health care settings

and wondering, well, what is the quality of care I'm getting in this setting versus another setting or another individual? In this case, you can program uniformity of expertise across these platforms. I want to give an idea of where current paradigms

of medical robotics are today. This is a da Vinci surgical system. It is a teleoperated surgical robot that has tools that go inside your body. And the surgeon operates these tools using a joystick console, as shown here. And the tools inside your

body move, basically, directly proportional to the movement of the surgeon. This robot has been around for well over 25, if not 30 years, at this point. And if we look at where the landscape of surgical robotics today, it's really exploded.

And this is just a snapshot of all the surgical robotics out there. There are a significantly higher number of robots that I couldn't put on the page. But the point I want to make is that all of these robots are teleoperated today.

They have zero inherent skill. The skill is coming from the surgeon. And it does make surgeons more precise and less tired. But what it doesn't do is it doesn't help us address the population crisis issue. It does not help us do more surgery.

And in fact, when you're doing robotic surgery, oftentimes the surgical team that's required to perform the procedure requires more personnel than if you were to do it without a robot. Now, if you look on the other side, where there is autonomous

robots being deployed, it's manufacturing. And in manufacturing, it's all rigid, preprogrammed motions. They operate in a very structured environment. They require extensive setup and human oversight. But they do excel at speed, precision, and repeatability.

This is autonomy but in an unskilled way. So what if we try to merge the concepts of autonomy and surgical robotics? This concept is actually not new at all. If you can believe it, this is concepts that have been dating back many decades, both from things

like ROBODOC that was used for orthopedic surgery and doing small alignments for implants, to AESOP, which is a voice-controlled robot that holds a surgical camera for laparoscopic surgery, to methods from university labs that have looked at using, what

is very popular today, concepts of imitation learning, or learning from demonstration, to show things like autonomous suturing. So all of this has been a progression of new techniques back in the day that have been applied over and over to try to address

this issue of surgical autonomy. And in certain cases, we've been able to show some successes. But if we look at where are we recently today in terms of general robot autonomy, we're looking at these ideas of large foundation models or

vision-language-action models, which usually require large data sets, which is massive data collection at scale, or developing what's called world models, like simulations or generative models of the world, that are trying to describe how

the world evolves over time. And what we see in this space right now is a large variability between accuracy and success. And so there's a lot of tasks that are shown that can be very successful at decent accuracies in the mid to high 90 percentage range.

But there's also many that are failing dramatically. And all of these foundation models have been developed in what I would say is relatively clean and controlled settings, where stakes are low. The environment can be easily reset

and for the tasks in which the demonstrators are abundant. So people that can sit down at a console and just show a robot how to fold a piece of laundry. Almost anybody can do that. But surgical robotics has that issue of none of those properties

really exist for surgery so that you have scarce data. The setting cannot be controlled. The setting cannot be easily reset. When you're doing a surgery, you can't roll back time normally. Safety is absolutely critical. So few demonstrators-- we already talked

about the lack of surgeons. So there's even fewer demonstrators, and there's very low incentives for them to be sitting and doing demonstrations for a robot learner. Data collection in these situations is basically at the lowest priority. You're usually trying

to address a patient and not to address the machine learning algorithm. And finally, world models right now have no concrete path to maturity. Given that there is a limited data, that data is protected behind and reasonably so behind privacy laws.

And so how else can we approach autonomy? And so we can look back at what I would say is the foundational pillars of autonomous robots. And I would say that there's four that I would categorize as-- one is perception, seeing and perceiving the world

and feeling the world. Second one is modeling and simulation, so understanding rough models of how things move, the general physics of the world at a small scale. Planning, understanding how to make decisions, given that you how the world

evolves, and then control, executing those actions in a precise way. And altogether, in various types of methods, we can bring these all together to get what we call embodied intelligence and autonomy. So at my lab at UC San Diego, we have

been playing around with these four pillars quite a lot and trying to build up the technology to make surgical autonomy possible. And we've looked at a large range of different areas of autonomous suturing to assistance, to deformable modeling and

probing to very specific robot applications, like biopsy and cancer. And I think what we've learned and what I feel like I've learned over the time is that at least one very viable path to unlocking autonomous, intelligent robots

in surgery is a structured path of building context awareness, moving towards incorporating multiple knowledge cues to build on this knowledge, to be a lifelong learner and then finding common embodiments so that we can deploy it at a larger scale.

So I want to cover these ideas during this talk. So for achieving context awareness, what I'm really talking about is perception. So robot autonomy, in my opinion, can only be as good as its perception and its ability to recognize and understand the world.

And only recently have we been able to get techniques very much on the backbone of large data collection and foundational models to segment the world, identify, localize, and track targets. These are just two examples of the state of the art.
